body.guess: Different TCP congestion controls respond differently to loss and delay; a loss-insensitive or bandwidth-estimating control such as TcpBbr may keep TCP closer to the bottleneck capacity than Cubic.
body.hypothesis: At l1.queue.length=100, at least one TCP congestion control other than TcpCubic gives tcp_goodput_bps more than 1% higher than the default while keeping udp_loss_frac <= 0.01.
body.because: The guess claims other controls perform better; the hypothesis tests if any alternative control achieves higher goodput with low loss, directly verifying this claim.

body.guess: The default queue length may be limiting TCP throughput; changing it, especially making it larger, could reduce TCP loss/backoff and increase TCP goodput, while making it smaller could also change loss behavior.
body.hypothesis: With TcpCubic, at least one tested queue length different from 100 packets (4, 10, 500, or 1000) gives tcp_goodput_bps more than 1% higher than the default while keeping udp_loss_frac <= 0.01.
body.because: The guess claims queue length limits TCP throughput, so testing if other lengths improve goodput directly validates this causal link.

body.result: Default Cubic gives 668.859 Mbps TCP goodput with 492 link drops and 294 TCP retransmissions.
body.guess: Cubic's loss-based congestion control backs off after queue drops, so useful TCP throughput is slightly below the capacity that the saturated link could otherwise carry.
body.unseen: The time series of cwnd, queue occupancy, and drop timing would show whether TCP repeatedly reduces its window after short queue-full periods.
body.matters: If loss-induced backoff is the cause, a setting that reduces loss or a less loss-sensitive TCP could raise tcp_goodput_bps.
body.reason: This makes a direct prediction that can be tested by changing tcp.type and queue length.
body.observations: E0 default run: tcp_goodput_bps=668859002, udp_loss_frac=0.000739, l1_util=1.0, l1_drops=492, tcp_retrans=294. The link is reported saturated, while UDP is a constant 300 Mbps flow. If UDP loss is allowed to rise only to 0.01, at most about 3 Mbps of UDP link bits can be freed, and the default TCP retransmission count is small (294 segments over 10 s, roughly a few tenths of a Mbps of payload). Therefore the most important unexplained thing is whether the apparent shortfall of TCP goodput from a simple 1 Gbps minus UDP calculation is caused by TCP loss/backoff/queue/algorithm choices, or whether it is already bounded by link capacity, packet overhead, and the UDP-loss constraint.

body.result: The default queue length is 100 packets and the run has non-zero drops.
body.guess: The default queue length may be limiting TCP throughput; changing it, especially making it larger, could reduce TCP loss/backoff and increase TCP goodput, while making it smaller could also change loss behavior.
body.unseen: The standing queue and the fraction of time the queue is full are not visible from the summary metrics.
body.matters: If queue length controls loss/backoff, l1.queue.length could be a useful knob for maximizing TCP goodput under the UDP-loss constraint.
body.reason: Queue length is one of the two allowed knobs and can be tested directly.

body.result: The default TCP congestion control is TcpCubic.
body.guess: Different TCP congestion controls respond differently to loss and delay; a loss-insensitive or bandwidth-estimating control such as TcpBbr may keep TCP closer to the bottleneck capacity than Cubic.
body.unseen: BBR's internal bandwidth and RTprop estimates, pacing rate, and probe behavior are not visible in the summary metrics.
body.matters: If algorithm choice matters, tcp.type could give a larger TCP goodput without changing queue length.
body.reason: All TCP choices can be compared at the default queue in one experiment.

body.result: l1_util is already 1.0, UDP is 300 Mbps, and the UDP-loss constraint allows only a small increase in UDP loss.
body.guess: The result may be hard-bounded by link capacity and the UDP flow: even eliminating TCP retransmissions and using the full allowed UDP loss may change TCP goodput by less than the 1% tolerance.
body.unseen: Exact packet overhead, UDP bits actually sent on the link, and the capacity available to TCP payload after headers are not directly reported.
body.matters: If this capacity-bound explanation is true, no allowed setting should make a meaningful difference, and the best recommendation may be the default.
body.reason: The TCP-type and queue-length tests will show whether any setting can exceed the 1% tolerance.

decision_rules.decision_rule: ((udp_loss_frac@TCP_NEWRENO <= 0.01) AND (tcp_goodput_bps@TCP_NEWRENO >= tcp_goodput_bps@DEFAULT * 1.01)) OR ((udp_loss_frac@TCP_LINUXRENO <= 0.01) AND (tcp_goodput_bps@TCP_LINUXRENO >= tcp_goodput_bps@DEFAULT * 1.01)) OR ((udp_loss_frac@TCP_BBR <= 0.01) AND (tcp_goodput_bps@TCP_BBR >= tcp_goodput_bps@DEFAULT * 1.01)) OR ((udp_loss_frac@TCP_VEGAS <= 0.01) AND (tcp_goodput_bps@TCP_VEGAS >= tcp_goodput_bps@DEFAULT * 1.01)) OR ((udp_loss_frac@TCP_BIC <= 0.01) AND (tcp_goodput_bps@TCP_BIC >= tcp_goodput_bps@DEFAULT * 1.01))
decision_rules.rival: All TCP congestion controls are already limited by the saturated 1 Gbps link and the 300 Mbps UDP flow, so no TCP type can raise TCP goodput by more than 1% while keeping UDP loss <= 1%.

decision_rules.decision_rule: ((udp_loss_frac@Q4 <= 0.01) AND (tcp_goodput_bps@Q4 >= tcp_goodput_bps@DEFAULT * 1.01)) OR ((udp_loss_frac@Q10 <= 0.01) AND (tcp_goodput_bps@Q10 >= tcp_goodput_bps@DEFAULT * 1.01)) OR ((udp_loss_frac@Q500 <= 0.01) AND (tcp_goodput_bps@Q500 >= tcp_goodput_bps@DEFAULT * 1.01)) OR ((udp_loss_frac@Q1000 <= 0.01) AND (tcp_goodput_bps@Q1000 >= tcp_goodput_bps@DEFAULT * 1.01))
decision_rules.rival: Queue length only changes delay and loss, not TCP goodput, because the link is already saturated; any queue change either leaves TCP within 1% of default or makes UDP loss exceed 1%.
